title: “THIS TOO SHALL PASS” — IS IT ACTUALLY IN THE BIBLE?
paragraphs:
“THIS TOO SHALL PASS” — IS IT ACTUALLY IN THE BIBLE?
The Four Words Christians Keep Quoting as Scripture… That Scripture Never Actually Says
“This too shall pass.”
Maybe someone whispered those words to you beside a hospital bed.
Maybe you repeated them after a relationship collapsed.
Maybe you typed them beneath someone’s post when you didn’t know what else to say.
Maybe you told yourself those four words while staring at a ceiling at 2:17 in the morning, wondering how much longer you could carry what nobody else knew you were carrying.
“This too shall pass.”
It sounds biblical.
It feels biblical.
It has been repeated so often in Christian conversations that many people assume there must be a verse somewhere that says exactly that.
There isn’t.
You can search the Psalms.
You can search Proverbs.
You can search the prophets.
You can search the words of Jesus.
You can search the letters of Paul.
You will find extraordinary promises about suffering, endurance, eternity, restoration, and the temporary nature of this present world.
But you will not find a Bible verse that simply says:
“This too shall pass.”
And strangely enough, discovering that does not make the Christian hope weaker.
It makes it stronger.
Because Christianity does not offer you a sentimental slogan promising that every painful circumstance will disappear exactly when you want it to.
Christianity gives you something infinitely greater.
It gives you Jesus Christ.
And there is an enormous difference between believing, “Eventually my circumstances will change,” and believing, “Even if my circumstances do not change today, Christ will not abandon me.”
Maybe that distinction is exactly what somebody reading this needs right now.
Because perhaps you have been waiting for “this” to pass.
The grief.
The loneliness.
The financial pressure.
The unanswered prayer.
The betrayal.
The consequences of your own mistakes.
The shame you cannot seem to silence.
The temptation that keeps returning.
The season where everybody thinks you are strong because they cannot hear what happens inside your head when the room gets quiet.
You keep saying:
“This too shall pass.”
But somewhere underneath those words is another question.
“When?”
And underneath that question may be another one.
“God… where are You?”
That is where a slogan reaches its limit.
And where Scripture begins speaking with far greater power.

Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 4:17–18 about suffering with language far more astonishing than “this too shall pass.” He called the believer’s present affliction temporary when measured against an eternal glory beyond comparison, and then directed our eyes beyond what can presently be seen.
The Greek makes the contrast especially vivid.
τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν… αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης
to gar parautika elaphron tēs thlipseōs hēmōn… aiōnion baros doxēs
Paul contrasts present θλῖψις — thlipsis, affliction, pressure, distress, with an αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης — aiōnion baros doxēs, an eternal weight of glory.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not pretend suffering does not hurt.
He does not tell grieving Christians to smile harder.
He does not reduce agony to a motivational quote.
He changes the scale.
Your suffering may feel enormous when measured against Tuesday.
It may feel unbearable when measured against this month.
It may feel endless when measured against the last three years.
But Paul measures present suffering against eternity.
And suddenly the equation changes.
Not because the suffering becomes imaginary.
Because eternity becomes enormous.
This is one of Christianity’s most radical claims:
The Christian does not ultimately overcome suffering because every earthly problem receives an earthly solution.
The Christian overcomes because suffering does not receive the final word.
Jesus does.
That matters, because some things do not simply “pass” in the neat way inspirational sayings imply.
Some people pray for healing and continue living with illness.
Some marriages are not restored.
Some prodigal children take years to return.
Some never return in this lifetime.
Some believers carry scars until death.
Some funerals leave an empty chair that remains empty.
Some consequences cannot be reversed.
Some apologies arrive too late.
Some doors never reopen.
Some questions remain unanswered on this side of eternity.
So biblical Christianity cannot merely promise:
“Hold on. Everything will eventually become comfortable again.”
Jesus never promised His disciples that.
In fact, He told them plainly:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation.”
But He did not stop there.
“...but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
That is John 16:33.
And the Greek word translated “tribulation” is again related to θλῖψις — thlipsis.
Pressure.
Affliction.
Distress.
Jesus did not say, “You might experience pressure if something goes wrong.”
He prepared His followers for it.
And then He grounded their courage not in the disappearance of trouble but in Himself:
ἐγὼ νενίκηκα τὸν κόσμον
egō nenikēka ton kosmon
“I have overcome the world.”
That is stronger than “this too shall pass.”
Because sometimes God removes the storm.
Sometimes God carries you through the storm.
And sometimes the storm continues long enough that you discover something about Christ you never would have learned standing beneath a cloudless sky.
There are people reading this who know exactly what that means.
You asked God to remove something.
Instead, He began changing you inside it.
You prayed for escape.
He started teaching endurance.
You begged Him to change another person.
He exposed something in your own heart.
You wanted relief.
He began producing repentance.
You wanted answers.
He gave you His presence.
You wanted the chapter erased.
Jesus began rewriting what the chapter meant.
That is the strange mathematics of grace.

God can take something Satan intended for destruction, something another person intended for harm, something the fallen world produced through suffering, or even something you created through your own sinful choices—and without ever calling evil good, God can redeem what seemed irredeemable.
Joseph understood something like this after being betrayed and sold by his own brothers.
Genesis 50:20 records his words:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
The Hebrew contains an extraordinary contrast.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
attem chashavtem alai ra‘ah; Elohim chashavah letovah
The same Hebrew root, חשב — chashav, appears in the contrast: what they intended or planned for evil, God intended for good.
God did not need Joseph’s brothers to have pure motives in order to accomplish His purposes.
Their evil remained evil.
Their guilt remained real.
Yet their sin was not sovereign.
God was.
Somebody needs to hear that distinction.
What happened to you may have been wrong.
What they did may actually have been evil.
What you did may actually require repentance.
Christianity does not require us to rename darkness as light.
Grace does something more astonishing.
It declares that darkness does not possess enough authority to prevent God from accomplishing His purposes.
And perhaps that is why Romans 8:28 has comforted suffering Christians for centuries.
“And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.”
That verse does not say all things are good.
Cancer is not good.
Abuse is not good.
Betrayal is not good.
Sin is not good.
Death is an enemy.
Paul’s claim is that God is capable of working through “all things” toward His redemptive purposes for His people.
And Romans 8 does not climax with Christians receiving easier circumstances.
It climbs toward something far greater.
Conformity to the image of Christ.
Then Paul moves through suffering, persecution, danger, and death before declaring that nothing in all creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is biblical hope.
Not:
“Nothing painful will happen.”
But:
“Nothing can separate me from Christ.”
Not:
“I will never cry again.”
But:
“My tears are not the final chapter.”
Not:
“I understand everything God is doing.”
But:
“I know the One holding me when I understand nothing.”
And this reaches all the way back into the Psalms.
Psalm 23 does not say:
“Because God is my shepherd, there will be no valley.”
David says:
“Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil…”
Why?
Not because valleys are imaginary.
Not because believers never suffer.
Not because every problem disappears overnight.
The center of David’s confidence is painfully simple:
“for thou art with me.”
כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי
ki attah immadi
“For You are with me.”
That may be one of the most important corrections to the popular phrase “this too shall pass.”
The deepest Christian comfort is not that “this” will pass.
It is that He is with you while you pass through it.
Read that again.
Because there is a difference.
A tremendous difference.
If your hope depends entirely upon circumstances changing, every delayed answer can feel like abandonment.
But when your hope is anchored in Christ, you can grieve and still worship.
You can hurt and still believe.
You can tremble and still pray.
You can say, “I don’t understand You, God,” without saying, “Therefore I will leave You.”
Faith is not pretending the valley is beautiful.
Faith is discovering that the Shepherd entered it with you.
And nowhere is that truth clearer than at the cross.
Christianity does not worship a distant God shouting encouragement toward suffering humanity from the safety of heaven.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
Jesus entered our broken world.
He experienced rejection.
Betrayal.
Injustice.
Mockery.
Physical agony.
And death.
At Calvary, the disciples could have looked at everything happening and concluded:
This is the end.
Their Messiah was crucified.
Their expectations shattered.
Their courage collapsed.
The One they believed would redeem Israel lay dead.
Saturday must have felt like proof that hope had failed.
But Saturday did not know Sunday was coming.
The stone was not the final punctuation mark.
The resurrection changed everything.
And here is where “this too shall pass” becomes almost embarrassingly small compared with the Gospel.
The Gospel does not merely announce that bad seasons eventually end.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ entered death itself and came out victorious.
Paul therefore taunts death in 1 Corinthians 15:
“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
The Greek word for victory is νῖκος — nikos.
Victory.
Triumph.
Conquest.
Death—the thing human beings cannot outrun, negotiate with, purchase their way out of, or permanently defeat—has met Someone stronger.
Jesus Christ.
So yes.
This world is passing.
Scripture actually says that.
First John 2:17 says:
“And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.”
Paul similarly writes in 1 Corinthians 7:31 that “the fashion of this world passeth away.”
Revelation eventually gives us the breathtaking destination toward which biblical hope moves: God dwelling with His people, death defeated, mourning ended, tears wiped away.
Revelation 21:4 declares:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying…”
So there is a profoundly biblical sense in which we can say that the present order of suffering will not last forever.
But Scripture gives that confidence a foundation.
Not fate.
Not positive thinking.
Not “the universe.”
Not karma.
Not time.
Christ.
This is why Christians should be careful with phrases that sound biblical.
A statement can contain a measure of truth without being Scripture.
And when we attach “the Bible says” to something the Bible never actually says, even accidentally, we blur the difference between human wisdom and the Word of God.
You do not need to make the Bible say something it never said in order to comfort somebody.
What Scripture actually says is better.
When you are shattered:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart…” — Psalm 34:18.
When you are afraid:
“What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.” — Psalm 56:3.
When you are exhausted:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28.
When you feel abandoned:
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” — Hebrews 13:5.
When suffering feels meaningless:
God is working toward purposes larger than what you presently see.
When death feels final:
Jesus says, “I am the resurrection, and the life…” — John 11:25.
Those promises do not need improvement.
But perhaps there is another reason this phrase matters.
Sometimes “this too shall pass” becomes our way of waiting for pain to disappear while avoiding what God wants to do in us through it.
We want the season to pass.
God wants the old person to pass away.
We want circumstances transformed.
God wants hearts transformed.
We want God to fix what hurts.
Sometimes God first confronts what is sinful.
Because not every difficult season is merely something to survive.
Some seasons expose us.
The argument exposed your pride.
The temptation exposed your divided heart.
The financial collapse exposed what you worshipped.
The loneliness exposed how desperately you needed human approval.
The scandal exposed what secrecy had protected.
The consequences exposed what compromise had been quietly building.
And suddenly the prayer changes.
It is no longer merely:
“God, make this pass.”
It becomes:
“Jesus, do not let me pass through this unchanged.”
That is a dangerous prayer.
Because Christ loves us too much merely to make us comfortable while leaving our idols untouched.
Maybe what needs to “pass” is not merely your suffering.
Maybe the hiding needs to pass.
The pornography needs to pass.
The bitterness needs to pass.
The secret messages need to pass.
The affair needs to pass.
The drunkenness needs to pass.
The hatred needs to pass.
The religious performance needs to pass.
The obsession with approval needs to pass.
The version of Christianity where Jesus is Savior but never Lord needs to pass.
Maybe you have spent months asking God to change your circumstances while the Holy Spirit has been putting His finger on your heart.
And you know it.
This is where the Gospel becomes uncomfortable before it becomes beautiful.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult seasons easier.
He came to save sinners.
He calls us to repentance.
He calls us away from sin and toward Himself.
And repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up sufficiently to earn mercy.
You cannot do that either.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience, died for sinners, and rose again victorious.
Forgiveness is not purchased by your tears.
Grace is not wages for good behavior.
Salvation is the gift of God received through faith in Christ.
And when Christ saves someone, He does not simply cover yesterday.
He begins transforming tomorrow.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes, not merely opportunities.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose stories appear permanently stained.
Then Jesus enters the story.
Scandal meets grace.
Shame meets mercy.
Sin meets the cross.
Death meets resurrection.
And suddenly what looked like the final chapter becomes the place where redemption begins writing.
That is our heartbeat:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because the past becomes good.
Not because Christians pretend scars never happened.
Because Jesus is capable of giving sinners something the world cannot manufacture:
forgiveness.
A new identity.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A new direction.
And ultimately resurrection life.
So if you are reading this while waiting for “this” to pass, perhaps your first prayer should not be:
“Lord, when will this end?”
Perhaps it should be:
“Lord Jesus, who are You calling me to become while I am here?”
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have sinned, repent.
If shame has convinced you that Jesus could never receive you, look again at the cross.
If you have fallen repeatedly, stop using grace as permission to remain down and start trusting grace as the power that calls you back to Christ.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, do not mistake familiarity with Christianity for reconciliation with God.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still need Christ.
You can attend church and still need Christ.
You can post Bible verses and still need Christ.
You can encourage everybody else and still desperately need Christ.
Come to Him.
Not after you repair yourself.
Now.
Bring the wreckage.
Bring the guilt.
Bring the questions.
Bring the secret nobody knows.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the failure you cannot undo.
Bring the heart you cannot heal.
Jesus is not intimidated by ruins.
He specializes in resurrection.
And perhaps that is what you really needed instead of four comforting words.
Not:
“This too shall pass.”
But:
Jesus Christ will remain.
Hebrews 13:8 says:
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.”
Your season changes.
Jesus remains.
People change.
Jesus remains.
Your strength changes.
Jesus remains.
Your emotions change.
Jesus remains.
Your circumstances change.
Jesus remains.
This world itself will pass away.
Jesus remains.
And if you belong to Him, your ultimate future is not determined by the chapter currently making you cry.
It is determined by the risen Christ.
If this exposed something you have been carrying quietly, do not turn the moment into another scroll and forget.
Be honest.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light is the first honest step after months of pretending.
And somewhere on your Facebook friends list is probably someone whose smile is hiding a war.
Not merely because you enjoyed it.
Send it privately to the friend who stopped talking about God.
Send it to the believer who is tired.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing more substantial to offer than religious slogans.
If this ministry is helping you grow closer to Christ, there is also a practical way to stand behind the work.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
God's favor cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So support Christian work because you want Christ proclaimed—not because you think giving money earns another ounce of God's love.
And tonight, when the room becomes quiet again…
when the problem is still there…
when the diagnosis has not changed…
when the person has not returned…
when the prayer still seems unanswered…
when you are tempted to whisper, “This too shall pass” just to survive another hour…
remember something stronger.
Maybe it will pass tomorrow.
Maybe it will take years.
Maybe some scars will remain until Jesus calls you home.
But if you are in Christ, the valley cannot keep you forever.
Sin will not have the final word.
Shame will not have the final word.
Your scandal will not have the final word.
Your suffering will not have the final word.
The grave will not have the final word.
Jesus will.
And when everything temporary has finally passed away, the One who carried you through every trembling chapter will still be standing.
Your pain may belong to this chapter—but Jesus has already secured the ending.
